html:
The capital that Emperor Kanmu founded in 794, the city now called Kyoto. It was the home of the emperor of Japan for over a thousand years, until the court moved to Tokyo after 1868.

Kanmu left Nara partly to escape the power of its great Buddhist temples. Like Nara, the new city copied the grid of the Chinese capital Chang'an, with a palace at the north end and a wide avenue running south. Its name means "capital of peace and calm", and it gave its name to the Heian period of Japanese history, 794 to 1185.

Its court nobles made a refined culture of poetry and fine manners. Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji here. The Gion Matsuri festival began here in 869.

Real power later moved to the warrior governments of the shoguns, and the city was badly burned in the Ōnin War of the 1460s and 1470s. It kept its place as the home of the emperor, of great temples such as Kinkaku-ji, and of the old arts.
